title: How To Build Instant Rapport With Individual Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin introduces isopraxism, an unconscious mirroring behavior common among close friends and couples, as a technique for putting individual students at ease during one-on-one conversations even when whole-class rapport comes easily. He warns against overtly friendly small talk, which can backfire and increase awkwardness, and clarifies that isopraxism isn't about copying visible mannerisms or slang but about matching a student's energy — pace, expression, and muscle tone — since teachers tend to operate at a higher frequency than students. He offers a simple practice: notice a student's energy before calling them over, then consciously mirror their calmer state, or use one's own calm to gently draw an anxious student down. He frames the technique as behaviorally grounded, if unconventional-sounding, and effective for making instruction land.

quotes: Isopraxism is a form of mirroring that happens naturally between friends and spouses.
If it’s inauthentic, if it isn’t you , then it will backfire every time. You’ll look ridiculous and your students will become even more painfully uncomfortable.
Teachers tend to operate at a high frequency. The heavy responsibility of the job can naturally pull you into a more heightened state.
Before calling over the student you want to speak to, take a moment to notice their energy and then simply lock into it.
If they seem apprehensive, however, then allow your own calm spirit to bring them into a softer, more open place. Just smile and breathe .
I know the strategy seems a bit out there, new-agey and woo-woo, but in the world of behavioral science it’s a proven and established method of inducing rapport.
